messages.author: 2a1ecf4da5e67f58
messages.subject: Spatial Logistic GLMM - Optimization
parts:
Hi,

I am trying to optimize a logistic GLMM, with a spatially correlated random effect. I am trying to fit the model with 9000 observations, but right now it won't run overnight using only 500 observations. I am a Stan beginner, and I have done my best with the manual, albeit without a deep understanding of why certain techniques improve efficiency/speed. Anyhow, I hope other users can help me improve my code and its efficiency. 

data {                             
  int<lower=0> N;                          // Number of observations
  int<lower=0> p;                           // number of predictors
  matrix[N,p] X;                              // Covariate matrix
  int<lower=0, upper=1> hit[N];     // 0/1 outcomes
  vector[2] px_pz[N];                     // (x, y) spatial coordinates
  vector[N] zero;                            // Random effect mean zero vector
}

parameters {                      
  real<lower=0> l;                    // covariance parameter
  real<lower = 0> sig;              // covariance parameter
  real beta0;                            // intercept 
  vector[p] beta;                      // predictor coefficients 
  vector[N] Z;                          // location mean random effect
}

model {   
  matrix[N, N] Sigma;
  Sigma = cov_exp_quad(px_pz, sig, l); 
  Sigma = cholesky_decompose(Sigma); 
  
  Z ~ multi_normal_cholesky(zero, Sigma);
  hit ~ bernoulli_logit(beta0 + X*beta + Z);
}

I am not proud, so I would greatly appreciate any and all feedback on my code for improving its overall quality, efficiency, and speed.

Thanks,

Chris

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Spatial Logistic GLMM - Optimization
parts:
I'm not sure but here are a couple quick guesses:
1.  Does X already have a constant term (a column of 1's)?  If so you will have a problem with your beta0 parameter because your betas all have flat priors.
2.  First check that your model works with Sigma as a simple diagonal matrix.
3.  I'm not completely up on how cov_exp_quad works, but I think the parameter "l" in your model is some sort of length scale, not a covariance parameter.  In any case, I think you'll need an informative prior on "l", which is fine as you must have prior information on this sort of parameter.
A

Try adding a small bit of diagonal noise to Sigma. Add code like below:

for (n in 1:N)
  Sigma[n, n] = Sigma[n, n] + 1e-6;

Before your line where you assign the Cholesky decomposition of Sigma to Sigma.

Also I would use the multivariate normal non centered parameterization here for Z rather than putting the multi_normal_cholesky prior on Z directly. 

Rob

messages.author: 89abf8a3796a510b
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Spatial Logistic GLMM - Optimization
parts:
On your question about length-scale: I would suggest using a distribution for l with a sharper tail, maybe a log-normal or a normal. If the data isn't informative about your length-scale, you'll need to pin it down with a prior. See if you can come up with plausible upper and lower bounds on your length-scale, and then use a distribution to put soft constraints on l. Without specifying stronger priors on l, you can run into trouble where your GP can act as a second constant term in your regression for large draws of length-scale and large draws of alpha. You should also put priors on sig for this reason. 

It'll also be good beta, and beta0. Make sure your x, y coordinates and your X variables are standardized, as it'll ensure that your parameters are all on the N(0, 1) scale. If you still have trouble, running a QR decomposition on your X variables and changing your likelihood to:

hit ~ bernoulli_logit(beta0 + Q*theta + Z_mod);

can also help the sampler run more efficiently. See here for more info: https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/p5vILNIgOYY/MPjb6foPBQAJ 


In general, it's hard to run complex models in Stan without specifying proper priors (rather than uniform, as you have here) for all your coefficients, especially if your coefficients are on different scales.


Rob

parts:
Hi again,

I decided to try the QR factorization. Does this look right to you?

data {                             
  int<lower=0> N;                        // Number of observations
  int<lower=0> p;                         // number of predictors

matrix[N,p] Q;                           // QR decomp - Q ***********************
  matrix[p,p] R;                            // QR decomp - R ***********************
  int<lower=0, upper=1> hit[N];   // 0/1 outcomes; array of integers
  vector[2] px_pz[N];                   // N-dim array of 2-dim vectors
}

parameters {                
  real<lower=0> l;                  // length-scale parameter
  real<lower = 0> sigma;       // scale parameter
  real beta0;                          // intercept 
  vector[p] theta;                   // ***********************
  vector[N] Z;                        // location random effect
}

transformed parameters {      // ***********************
      vector[p] beta;                 // ***********************
      beta = inverse(R)*theta;  // ***********************

}

model {  
  matrix[N, N] Sigma;
  vector[N] Z_mod;

l ~ lognormal(-2,1);                  
      sigma ~ lognormal(-1.5, 1.5);   
      beta0 ~ normal(0,5);
      beta ~ normal(0,5);                  // N(0,5) priors on all beta
      
      Sigma = cov_exp_quad(px_pz, sigma, l);

for (n in 1:N)
        Sigma[n, n] = Sigma[n, n] + 1e-6;

Sigma = cholesky_decompose(Sigma); 
      
      Z ~ normal(0, 1);  // Each element is N(0,1)
      Z_mod = Sigma * Z; // (Cov matrix Cholesky)*MVN(0,1)
      
      hit ~ bernoulli_logit(beta0 + Q*theta + Z_mod);  // ***********************
}

It is significantly faster, but the estimates seem different by non-trivial amounts. Do you see any mistakes or errors?

Thanks,

Chris
On Wednesday, November 23, 2016 at 1:10:57 PM UTC-8, Rob Trangucci wrote:

On your question about length-scale: I would suggest using a distribution for l with a sharper tail, maybe a log-normal or a normal. If the data isn't informative about your length-scale, you'll need to pin it down with a prior. See if you can come up with plausible upper and lower bounds on your length-scale, and then use a distribution to put soft constraints on l. Without specifying stronger priors on l, you can run into trouble where your GP can act as a second constant term in your regression for large draws of length-scale and large draws of alpha. You should also put priors on sig for this reason. 

It'll also be good beta, and beta0. Make sure your x, y coordinates and your X variables are standardized, as it'll ensure that your parameters are all on the N(0, 1) scale. If you still have trouble, running a QR decomposition on your X variables and changing your likelihood to:

hit ~ bernoulli_logit(beta0 + Q*theta + Z_mod);

can also help the sampler run more efficiently. See here for more info: https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/p5vILNIgOYY/MPjb6foPBQAJ 


In general, it's hard to run complex models in Stan without specifying proper priors (rather than uniform, as you have here) for all your coefficients, especially if your coefficients are on different scales.
Rob

For style in something like this, I prefer to see constants
that have fixed values defined in the transformed data block
so it's transparent what they are from looking at only the
Stan program.  But in this case, you're going to want to
just get rid of this variable, because...

> }
> parameters {

>   vector[N] Z;                      // location mean random effect
> }
> model {
>   matrix[N, N] Sigma;
>   vector[N] Z_mod;
>
>   Sigma = cov_exp_quad(px_pz, sig, l);                // Squared exponential cov matrix
>   for (n in 1:N)
>     Sigma[n, n] = Sigma[n, n] + 1e-6;                     // add noise to diagonal
>   Sigma = cholesky_decompose(Sigma);
>
>   Z_mod = Sigma * Z;                                            // Transform Standard MVN to Correlated MVN
>
>   l ~ gamma(0.5,1);

"l" is a suboptimal variable name because it's confusable with
"1" in many fonts (though not in a font a programmer would use,
of course :-)).

>
>   Z ~ multi_normal_cholesky(zero, I_N);               // Standard MVN

This is where you just want to do this:

  Z ~ normal(0, 1);

That puts an independent standard normal on each component of Z.

- Bob

>
> I decided to try the QR factorization. Does this look right to you?
> It is significantly faster, but the estimates seem different by non-trivial amounts. Do you see any mistakes or errors?

I don't know about QR specifically, but you want to measure
whether the posterior means are within a couple MCMC standard errors
of each other. The interfaces report these, but they're just
posterior std dev divided by sqrt of the effective sample size.

This is assuming that both approaches pass
convergence diagnostics run with multiple diffuse inits.

- Bob
